meta.subtitle: A premium regulated-and-renewables utility with a pending Dominion merger and data-center demand as a new tailwind

analystSentiment.commentary: NextEra Energy is two businesses under one holding company: Florida Power & Light, a regulated utility that earns a return on a growing rate base, and NextEra Energy Resources, a leading developer of wind, solar, and storage in the country. Together they have delivered years of steady, rate-base-driven earnings growth, and management targets an 8%-plus compound annual growth rate in adjusted earnings per share through 2032. The shares trade at $80.14, about 18.2x FY27E earnings and 17.5x EV/EBITDA — a growth multiple that the earnings guide has to justify. We rate NEE BUY with a $75–$108 target range and a probability-weighted fair value modestly below the $98.39 consensus target. Three things drive the case: FPL's rate-base growth now has a new driver in data-center demand (management cites roughly 21 GW of large-load interest), NEER's renewables backlog stands near 35.1 GW, and the pending combination with Dominion Energy would add scale and, management argues, support 9%-plus EPS growth through 2032. The offsetting risks are equally concrete: the Dominion deal must clear a long regulatory review, NEER's economics depend on federal clean-energy incentives that policy could curtail, and at $95B of total debt the balance sheet is sensitive to interest rates. The Street leans positive — 12 of 20 analysts rate the stock Buy — but the wide $55–$114 target range is the honest signal that the merger and the policy backdrop, not the operating business, are what the outcome turns on.

executiveSummary.companyOverview: NextEra Energy, founded in 1925 and headquartered in Juno Beach, Florida, operates through two segments: Florida Power & Light (FPL), a regulated electric utility serving roughly 12 million people through about 6 million customer accounts, and NextEra Energy Resources (NEER), a clean-energy generator and developer of wind, solar, nuclear, and battery storage. As of December 31, 2025 the company had about 35,963 megawatts of net generating capacity and roughly 93,000 circuit miles of transmission and distribution lines. The financial profile is that of a large, capital-intensive utility: FY25 revenue of $27.4B (+10.7%), a 30.2% operating margin, $14.9B of EBITDA, and $6.8B of net income ($3.30 diluted EPS), funded by $95B of total debt against $66.5B of equity. FPL grows by investing in its rate base through a large annual capital program, while NEER grows a contracted renewables backlog. The story now has two accelerants the utility sector has rarely seen: hyperscaler data-center demand and a pending merger with Dominion Energy.

thesis.label: BUY
thesis.body: NextEra is a bet that a genuine growth engine inside a low-growth sector keeps compounding through a rising-rate, shifting-policy environment. The bull case is structural: FPL earns a regulated return on a rate base swelling with data-center load, NEER converts a 35.1 GW backlog into contracted cash flows, and the Dominion combination adds scale at a target of 9%-plus EPS growth. The bear case is that a premium multiple leaves no cushion if the merger stalls in regulatory review, if federal clean-energy incentives are curtailed, or if $95B of debt meets higher-for-longer rates. We think the growth and the demand tailwind win over a multi-year horizon, but the premium valuation makes this a BUY on quality and catalysts rather than on a wide margin of safety.

catalysts: Regulatory approval of the proposed merger with Dominion Energy, which management says would support roughly 11% annual growth in regulatory capital employed and the accelerated EPS-growth target discussed above.

Conversion of FPL's large-load pipeline — management cites about 21 GW of data-center and other large-customer interest, with 12 GW in advanced discussions — into signed tariff agreements, with at least one expected by year-end.
Execution of NEER's renewables and storage backlog, and the return of the Duane Arnold nuclear plant to service by early 2029.
Continued delivery against the 8%-plus adjusted-EPS growth target off the 2025 base, which underpins the premium multiple.
risks: Merger risk: the Dominion combination faces a lengthy multi-agency regulatory review and may be delayed, blocked, or approved on unfavorable terms.
Policy risk: NEER's returns depend on federal clean-energy tax incentives, which recent legislation could reduce.
Rate and leverage risk: the company's large debt load means higher-for-longer interest rates raise financing costs and pressure the premium valuation.
Regulatory risk: FPL's earnings depend on the Florida Public Service Commission allowing timely cost recovery and a reasonable return on capital.

income.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.incomeCommentary: NextEra's income statement shows steady, rate-base-driven growth rather than the volatility of an unregulated business. Revenue rose from $17.1B in FY21 to $27.4B in FY25, a 10.7% gain in the latest year, and the operating margin has run near 30% in the last two years (30.2% in FY25) as regulated returns and contracted renewables scaled. FY25 EBITDA was $14.9B and net income $6.8B, for $3.30 of diluted EPS. There is no gross-profit line — a utility reports operating revenues against operating expenses, so gross margin is not a meaningful figure here and operating margin carries profitability. The most recent quarter continued the pattern: Q2'26 revenue of $7.5B was up 12.4% year over year at a 29.7% operating margin, and the company reported GAAP net income of $3.144 billion, or $1.50 per share, up from $0.98 a year earlier, with adjusted earnings of $1.15 per share (up 9.5%). Note that net income is flattered by production tax credits on renewables and by gains at NEER, so the reported net margin overstates the underlying operating profitability; we anchor on operating margin and the adjusted-EPS trajectory. Consensus looks for revenue of $31.1B in FY26E and $34.7B in FY27E, with EPS of $4.05 then $4.39 — the mid-single-to-high-single-digit compounding the valuation pays for.

balance.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.balanceCommentary: The balance sheet is heavily levered, as a capital-intensive regulated utility's is by design. NextEra closed FY25 with $95B of total debt and $2.8B of cash and short-term investments, leaving net debt of $92.2B against $66.5B of equity, and trailing net debt to EBITDA of about 6.7x. For an industrial company that figure would be alarming; for a utility earning a regulated return on rate base and long-term contracted cash flows it is normal, and NextEra funds it with investment-grade access to capital. The trailing current ratio of 0.53 is likewise typical of a utility that finances long-lived assets with long-term debt rather than working capital. The real risk in the leverage is not solvency but sensitivity to interest rates: with debt of this size, a higher-for-longer rate path raises the cost of the continuous refinancing and new issuance the growth plan requires, and can compress an equity multiple that has priced in growth — the Dominion merger would add further scale and financing needs on top. This rate sensitivity is the thread that runs through the risk section below. The balance sheet supports the growth so long as capital markets stay open on reasonable terms.

cashflow.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.cashflowCommentary: Cash generation is strong at the operating line and fully consumed by investment. Operating cash flow reached $12.5B in FY25, up from $7.6B in FY21 as the business scaled. Capital expenditure and free cash flow are not shown here because NextEra tags capital spending under company-specific line items rather than a standard cash-flow concept, but the scale is clear from disclosure: FPL alone plans $12–$13B of capital investment this year, and NextEra as a whole spends more than it generates — free cash flow is structurally negative for a utility building rate base ahead of the returns it will earn. The dividend is the shareholder's near-term reward: FY25 dividends paid were $4.7B, a 3.05% yield, and the payout has grown every year (from $3.0B in FY21). The pattern is deliberate — outspend operating cash flow to grow the asset base, fund the gap with debt and equity, and return a rising dividend — and it works only while the regulated returns and contracted cash flows validate the spending.

multiples.note: Peer multiples pending a peer data source.

valuation.multiplesCommentary: NextEra carries a growth multiple, and whether it is deserved is the whole valuation question. The shares change hands at 17.5x EV/EBITDA and 5.8x sales, and on earnings at about 19.8x the next twelve months and 18.2x FY27E as consensus EPS compounds. For a utility — an asset class usually valued for its yield and steady rate-base growth — those are full multiples, but they are not demanding against management's 8%-to-9% adjusted-EPS growth guide: a roughly 18x forward multiple on high-single-digit earnings growth is a reasonable price if the growth is delivered. The multiple can be defended only if that growth continues and if the Dominion merger and the data-center demand deliver; it is not a margin of safety. The Street is constructively positive: 20 analysts split Buy 12, Hold 7, Sell 1, with a consensus target of $98.39 — about 22.8% above the $80.14 price — and a median of $100.50. The range tells the real story: from $55.00 to $114.00, a wide spread for a company this stable, and that width is a referendum on the merger and the clean-energy policy backdrop, not on FPL's rate base.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: The growth accelerants deliver: the Dominion merger is approved on favorable terms and proves accretive, FPL converts its large-load pipeline into signed data-center tariffs, NEER executes its backlog, and clean-energy incentives hold. Earnings compound at the high end of the 9%-plus target, the growth multiple is sustained or expands, and the shares re-rate toward the top of the Street's range near the $114 high target.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: The standalone plan is delivered — roughly 8% adjusted-EPS growth off the 2025 base — and the merger progresses through its regulatory review without a clean resolution inside the year. Revenue and earnings track the consensus path, the multiple holds rather than expands, and the shares appreciate toward the consensus target as the dividend compounds.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: The premium unwinds. The Dominion merger is delayed, blocked, or repriced; federal clean-energy incentives are curtailed, cutting NEER's project returns; or a higher-for-longer rate path lifts financing costs and compresses a utility multiple that had priced in growth. Earnings still grow, but slower, and the stock de-rates to a new low, below its 52-week trough.

valuation.scenarioCommentary: Probability-weighting the three cases gives a fair value of about $94, roughly 17% above the current price — the arithmetic behind a BUY, and one that sits just below the consensus target. We weight the Base case at 45% because a delivered standalone plan with an unresolved-but-progressing merger is the most likely path for a large, closely-regulated company, and split the tails toward the bull (30%) over the bear (25%): the data-center demand and the backlog make continued growth more probable than a stall, but the merger-approval and policy risks are real enough to keep the bear case a genuine scenario. The $75–$108 target range brackets the Base outcome and excludes both tails, which hinge on multi-year regulatory and policy outcomes the next few quarters cannot settle. An investor's stance should turn on their read of the merger and the clean-energy policy backdrop more than on FPL's rate base, which is the dependable part.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: NextEra reports as a single consolidated line ($27.4B of FY25 revenue), but it is economically two businesses, and the quarter's disclosure shows both. Florida Power & Light, the regulated utility, reported Q2'26 net income of $1.412 billion ($0.67 per share) and grew its regulatory capital employed by roughly 9.3% year over year — the dependable, rate-base engine. NextEra Energy Resources, the clean-energy developer, reported Q2'26 GAAP net income of $1.634 billion ($0.78 per share) and added 3.6 GW to a backlog that now totals about 35.1 GW, including battery storage — the growth engine, but one exposed to policy and merchant dynamics the regulated side is not. The single-segment presentation understates that structural split; the two halves grow differently and carry different risks, and the report treats them as one only because the FactPack does.

moatFactors.name: Regulated monopoly (FPL)
moatFactors.body: FPL is a regulated electric monopoly serving roughly 12 million people in a growing state, earning a Florida-commission-set return on a rate base it keeps expanding. Its scale and operating efficiency — management notes a typical residential bill about 30% below the national average and non-fuel operating costs well below the industry — let it invest heavily while keeping bills low, which supports constructive regulatory treatment. This is a durable, low-risk earnings base.

moatFactors.name: Renewables development scale (NEER)
moatFactors.body: NEER is a leading developer of wind, solar, and storage in the country, and scale is a real advantage in a business where supply chain, financing, interconnection queues, and development expertise gate returns. Its national-scale backlog and the technology and balance sheet to build all forms of energy give it a structural edge as power demand accelerates — provided the policy support for clean energy holds.

moatFactors.name: Data-center demand access
moatFactors.body: Both segments are positioned to capture the surge in large-load, data-center power demand — FPL through its tariff (roughly 21 GW of interest, 12 GW in advanced discussions) and NEER through contracted generation. This is a new, structural tailwind that a well-sited utility with capacity to build is unusually able to monetize, and it lengthens the growth runway.

moatFactors.name: Balance-sheet scale and capital access
moatFactors.body: Building rate base and renewables at this pace requires continuous access to low-cost capital, and NextEra's size, investment-grade standing, and financing expertise are themselves a competitive advantage over smaller developers. The same balance sheet that carries $95B of debt is what funds a capital program of this size, and is a stated rationale for the Dominion combination.

businessMoat.durability: NextEra's moat is wide and, unusually for a utility, still widening. The regulated FPL base is about as durable an earnings stream as exists in the market, and the renewables platform adds a growth dimension unusual for a utility. The durability qualifier is policy and rates, not competition: NEER's returns lean on clean-energy incentives that legislation can change, and the whole enterprise is financed with debt that reprices as rates move. Those are macro and political exposures rather than a narrowing of the competitive position. We rate the moat WIDE — the regulated monopoly and the development-scale advantage are real and lasting — while noting that the premium the market pays assumes the policy and rate backdrop stays supportive enough for the growth to continue.

points: Management targets 8%-plus adjusted-EPS compound annual growth through 2032 off the 2025 base, and the same rate from 2032 through 2035 — a long, explicitly-dated growth runway anchored to a single stated base.
FPL's rate base is expanding with disciplined capital investment, and data-center load is a new driver: about 21 GW of large-customer interest, with a first tariff transaction expected by year-end.
NEER is converting a roughly 35.1 GW backlog of renewables and storage into contracted cash flows, with 3.6 GW added in the quarter including 2 GW of battery storage.
The pending Dominion Energy combination would add scale across four fast-growing states and, per management, support roughly 11% annual regulatory-capital growth and 9%-plus EPS growth through 2032.
Transmission is a third leg: NextEra Energy Transmission energized a new line in New Mexico and was selected for large 765-kilovolt projects in Illinois, expanding a regulated growth avenue.
Consensus embeds the plan, modeling a steady climb in revenue and EPS through FY27E — the rising path the valuation already reflects.

management.leadership: John Ketchum serves as chairman, president, and chief executive officer, and the quarter's results and the Dominion transaction are being executed under his leadership. The company frames itself as a national leader in renewable-energy generation with the scale, supply chain, development expertise, and balance sheet to build all forms of energy — a strategy that has produced years of steady earnings growth. The leadership team is executing a coherent plan: grow FPL's rate base while keeping customer bills low, scale NEER's contracted renewables, capture data-center demand, and pursue the Dominion combination for additional scale. The execution record supports confidence in the operating plan; the open questions are external — regulatory approval of the merger and the policy backdrop for clean energy.
management.capitalAllocation: Capital allocation is built around growth investment funded by debt, equity, and retained cash, with a rising dividend as the shareholder return. FPL's large annual capital program, and NextEra's spending well beyond its operating cash flow, go to grow rate base and the renewables backlog ahead of the returns those assets will earn. The dividend has increased every year — the rising payout noted above — and the proposed Dominion merger, which would direct $2.25 billion in shareholder-funded bill credits to Dominion customers, is the defining capital-allocation decision on the table. The discipline is in matching spending to regulated and contracted returns; the risk is that the plan depends on continuous access to capital markets on reasonable terms.
management.governance: A DEF 14A proxy was captured and grounds the governance view. The board is majority-independent — all 11 non-employee directors were determined independent under NYSE standards — and maintains an independent Lead Director. The company combines the chairman and CEO roles in John Ketchum, a structure some investors prefer to see split; the board defends it as promoting unified leadership and offsets it with the independent Lead Director. A standing related-person-transactions policy governs dealings above $120,000, and the related-party item noted is minor (a director's son-in-law employed by a subsidiary). Nothing in the captured excerpt points to a governance red flag, though the combined chair/CEO role is worth monitoring.
management.insiderOwnership: The proxy excerpt captured here covers board independence, leadership structure, and the related-person policy, but does not quantify director or officer share ownership, so no insider-ownership percentage is asserted.

idiosyncratic: Merger execution: the proposed Dominion Energy combination requires approvals from multiple state and federal agencies and could be delayed, blocked, or approved on terms that reduce its benefit; the wide analyst target range reflects this uncertainty.

Clean-energy policy: NEER's project economics depend on federal tax incentives and supportive policy, and the company flags that recent legislation and related actions could reduce that support, raising costs or reducing returns on new projects.

Interest-rate and financing risk: as the balance-sheet discussion sets out, the scale of the debt and the continuous new issuance the plan requires leave both results and the equity multiple exposed to a higher-for-longer rate path.

Regulatory recovery: FPL's earnings depend on the Florida Public Service Commission permitting timely recovery of costs and a reasonable return on invested capital, which is not guaranteed and can be affected by political and economic conditions.
Valuation: the shares carry a growth multiple with limited cushion if any of the above disappoints, even as the underlying business keeps growing.
risks.systemic: NextEra is exposed to the macro and policy forces that move the whole utility sector, amplified by its size and growth ambitions. Interest rates are the dominant one: utilities are long-duration, debt-financed businesses, and NextEra's scale magnifies that sector-wide exposure. Energy and commodity prices, supply-chain availability for turbines, panels, and batteries, and the pace of electricity-demand growth all bear on the plan. Above all, the business is shaped by government policy — the regulatory compacts that set FPL's returns and the federal incentives that underpin NEER's renewables — so shifts in the political and legislative environment around energy can move results in either direction. These are sector-wide exposures, but NextEra carries them with heavy leverage and a valuation that embeds growth, which cuts both ways: more upside if the backdrop stays supportive, more to lose if it does not.

body: We rate NextEra Energy BUY with a $75–$108 target range and a probability-weighted fair value of about $94, roughly 17% above the $80.14 price and just below the $98.39 consensus. This is a BUY on a utility with a genuine growth story: a regulated Florida monopoly compounding its rate base, the country's leading renewables developer converting a large backlog, a new data-center demand tailwind, and a pending Dominion merger that would add scale behind an 8%-to-9% EPS growth target. The premium multiple is defensible against that growth, and the 3% dividend pays the investor to wait.

The discipline is that the premium leaves little margin for error, and the swing factors are external rather than operational. The Dominion merger must clear a long regulatory review, clean-energy incentives sit in a shifting policy environment, and the leverage keeps the equity sensitive to rates. We would add on any pullback that does not impair the growth plan, and would grow cautious on a merger setback, a material cut to clean-energy incentives, or evidence that rising financing costs are outrunning rate-base returns. For an investor who wants utility stability with genuine growth, NextEra is a leading way to own that combination; the price asks that the growth, and the policy backdrop behind it, hold.
